searchText: Thinking more on the random merge date... we have access to timestamps so we *could* assert that the merge will happen on the first block after UTC 14:00 on a random day. Developers would have to "watch for The Merge" every day, but at least it would be for a limited period of time each day. We could even say that it will always be on a Wednesday pretty easily. So every Wednesday everyone would watch for the first block with a 14:00 timestamp to see if The Merge happens. One caveat here is that miners could specifically avoid publishing any block they mine that would lead to the random block selection system deciding it is the merge block. This assumes that the blockhash is part of the random selection which I think is necessary unfortunately. Hmm, maybe we could have PoS decide (via RANDAO) whether to trigger or not each day without using the blockhash as input. by PoS you mean the beacon chain? Yeah. That'd be better in the case of random date selection. But we can't make the selection period too long, even a month would be too long, right? And if there is an announcement that the merge happens during the next month but we don't know when exactly it would not save us from miners preparing 51% attack or making a fork. It would only address the "last miner" problem but it could be addressed without randomizing the point of merge, by e.g. deferring the decision on the block to the beacon chain. I think if the random selection period is long *enough* then it addresses other miner attack vectors (like double spends). As an extreme example, if the period was 1 year I don't think miners would burn a years worth of income out of malice. I think the question we need to ask is if the duration required for miners to not behave maliciously is longer than the longest duration core devs would accept. I suspect core devs wouldn't be particularly happy with the fork happening "on a random Wednesday at 14:00 UTC sometime in about the next year". Wouldn't the same be achieved by maintaining a block reward for miners inside the ETH 2.0 after the merge for the same period (2 months for example)? Miners wouldn't have a direct incentive to fork at the merge because they would still be paid, and after it forking should be far more difficult (because at this point they don't do anything, they just get paid). Something like this should have far less uncertainty and complexity than having a random date. I am not worried at all about miners maintaining a non-PoS chain, and I do not think that is something we should try to prevent or do anything about. It is how fork-based governance works and is heathy. The fear is miners *attacking* the chain. You do make a valid point, if we are going to pay for PoW + PoS in either case, we might as well run PoS and just pay for PoW for the period. > The fear is miners attacking the chain. But it's kind of the same, if we keep paying miners 2 months after the merge there isn't much incentive to attack the chain either Requires more work to continue to pay miners on the beacon chain post-merge though. Does it? if we know the amount of time the PoW is going to live after the merge, then we can reduce the changes to a single event "mint x ETH to the PoW distribution contract". The contract can be written in solidity and distribute rewards to miners using those funds, without having any more changes to the consensus or anything like that. That contract would need to process PoW submissions. And have a difficulty adjustment algorithm. Basically rewrite Ethash PoW consensus inside a contract. Definitely possible I think, but I don't believe it will be simple. I understand working on that contract and on that unique event is going to require some work, but if it's not consensus critical it should be less than doing a random merge. If the contract has an error it's bad, but not so bad, it just breaks something that's not really consensus related. Miners can be responsible for the audit. (They are the only ones that care if the contract works well or it doesn't, from the chain perspective the funds are already spent) Rather than get miners to actually mine, it could be based on historical information. Take the last 3 month's of blocks and hard-code the distributions according to that. Then miners will be able to leave and still get rewards We specifically *need* them to mine though. or attack and get rewards 🤔 Actually, maybe <@144468805697929216> is right here. The real incentive not to attack is because you have a source of future-ETH, not that you are working for it. If you have Ethereum mining hardware, you have a "source of future ETH" so you don't attack the network today because you don't want to burn your future ETH. If someone asked, "can I rent your hashing power at a 10% premium for an hour so I can use it to attack Ethereum" most miners would say no, because that hurts the future-value of their mining hardware. So, if we pick a bunch of people who have mining hardware and we tell them, "we'll give you X ETH in a year" they have incentive to try to keep ETH's price high for at least a year. They could still gamble it thinking the attack is not going to be successful, it's a prisoners dilemma, from the individual perspective it's always better to get the free rewards and attack the network. Maintaining the PoW requires the hardware to be occupied, and not be available for an attack at all. It certainly isn't as strong as a guarantee, since having them do PoW, since they could sell their hardware (to a potential attacker) not realizing that it could hurt their future assets. ETH airdrop after some period of time post-merge is considered as one of the options to pay miners who continues to do PoW up to a certain block. It's easy to implement, main issue is that there must be an authority that is trusted and willing to spend ETH for this purpose. We *could* do an in-protocol system that doesn't require a wealthy trusted actor. That is the thing I was saying would have high engineering cost. I think we can mint new ETH for that period, and use a smart contract that handles the rewards and difficulty adjustment. There are multiple mineable ERC20s that already have some logic implemented. The biggest risk is "what happen if it's broken a ton of ETH get's minted", that shouldn't be an issue if we make the mint an unique event and let a contract distribute the funds. If the PoW contract is broken, well, then the mechanism breaks before it was expected and PoW dies earlier, not ideal but the protocol is not affected. My point being, we can split the work in two different parts: 1) Mint the ETH, this is risky but it has very low engineering cost 2) Distribute the ETH, this is less risky because all ETH required has already been minted and consensus doesn't depend from this, it has higher engineering cost but it's not as mission critical If the value of Eth that is distributed to miners is known, anyone can bid x+1 to attack pre merge. The rewards need to happen on eth2 imo the rewards, if they happen, should happen post-merge after decent amount of time We need to set the reward high enough that `x+1` is a sufficiently large number. Basically we are paying miners to lock up their hardware (not put it on the open market), and PoW becomes "Proof of not Selling Hardware". right, but if the rewards are known, anyone can bid x+1. Many competitors have the money , binance for example. Anyone can do that today, it is a known problem with PoW (and PoS as well for the most part). true, but eth2 tries to set a end date for miners, so there is less at stake for them the closer we get to such date I get it. But's the tragedy of the commons, miners by themselves still have incentives to attack + educating X miners how to withdraw their funds and use a validator 😅 Pools wouldn't need to get their users to validate, just the pool itself. If the merge takes 1 month more because we are thinking of better ways to handle the miners then we are already worse off than just paying them inside ETH 2.0 doesn't that make eth2 more complicated? skipping the validator queue?
